analysis.one_liner: Restores regulation of cable TV rates and forces cable systems to carry local broadcast stations.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 340-73 on July 23, 1992; Congress passed its companion bill, President George H.W. Bush vetoed it, and Congress overrode the veto, so the cable law took effect.
analysis.plain_summary: After the 1984 Cable Act deregulated cable rates in about 97 percent of franchises, cable operators raised prices on subscribers who in most places had no alternative provider. This bill lets the FCC or local franchising authorities cap the rates of cable systems that face no effective competition, bans charging customers for channels they never ordered, sets customer-service standards, and requires cable systems to carry local broadcast and public TV channels. It also opens programming controlled by cable operators to satellite and other competing distributors.
analysis.who_benefits: Cable subscribers in areas where the cable system faces no competition, who get basic-tier rate caps and refund procedures for unreasonable charges; viewers who rely on free over-the-air broadcast channels, which must be carried on cable; public and educational TV stations; subscribers, who can no longer be billed for pay channels or pay-per-view they never ordered; and hearing-impaired subscribers, for whom the bill requires compatible equipment.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Cable subscribers and local TV stations

how_it_helps.text: Re-establishes rate regulation: where the FCC finds a cable system is not subject to effective competition, local franchising authorities or the FCC can cap basic-tier rates using cost-based formulas, and reduce rates found unreasonable.
Bans negative-option billing, so an operator cannot charge a subscriber for an individually priced channel or pay-per-view program the subscriber never affirmatively requested.

Requires cable operators to carry the signals of local commercial stations and qualified noncommercial educational (public TV) stations, without degrading them or taking payment for carriage, so free over-the-air TV reaches homes that cannot receive broadcast signals with an antenna.

Sets FCC customer-service standards covering office hours, installations, outages, and billing and refunds, and lets states and franchising authorities enforce consumer protection laws and stricter customer-service rules.

Bars cable-affiliated programming vendors from unreasonably refusing to deal with competing multichannel distributors such as satellite providers, including a rule against exclusive contracts that deny programming to rural areas not served by cable.
Requires FCC rules so cable scrambling and converter boxes do not disable TV and VCR features, and requires equipment necessary for hearing-impaired subscribers.

analysis.who_pays: Cable operators and their shareholders bear the cost: rate caps, must-carry obligations, customer-service standards, equipment-compatibility rules, and billing restrictions all reduce their pricing power and flexibility. Some compliance costs can be passed to subscribers, and the retransmission-consent provision lets broadcast stations instead demand payment from cable systems, a cost operators can pass along in later years.

drawbacks.text: Rate regulation reaches only systems the FCC finds lack 'effective competition,' and regulating cable programming service rates happens through a complaint-driven process with limits on complaints about pre-existing rates, so relief can be slow and partial.
Must-carry obliges operators with more than 12 channels to devote up to one-third of channel capacity to local commercial stations, capacity that is then unavailable for other programming services.

Retransmission consent gives each local broadcast station a choice between guaranteed free carriage and the right to charge cable systems for its signal; an honest supporter would acknowledge that broadcasters choosing cash creates a cost that cable operators can pass to subscribers.

The House bill itself directed the FCC to study whether its own subscriber-protection rules impose unreasonable costs on operators or subscribers, an acknowledgment of compliance costs built into the design.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill responded to a documented problem: Congress's own findings say the 1984 act deregulated rates in about 97 percent of franchises and that a minority of operators abused that status by unreasonably raising rates [S5]. The rate caps, billing protections, and must-carry rules delivered direct, tangible relief to subscribers, at a real cost to the cable industry and some lost channel flexibility. The bill's biggest long-term design trade-off is retransmission consent, which gave broadcasters a revenue lever that cable operators could later pass on to subscribers as retransmission fees. On balance the consumer protections were substantial and the costs were borne mostly by the regulated industry.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 340-73, the Senate passed a companion bill, President George H.W. Bush vetoed it, and Congress voted to override the veto in October 1992, so the law took effect over the president's objection.

narrative.text: The House passed the bill 340-73 on July 23, 1992, with 241 of 265 voting Democrats and 98 of 166 voting Republicans in favor.
After House passage, the bill was laid on the table with action pointed to S. 12, the Senate companion measure.
President George H.W. Bush vetoed the cable bill in October 1992, and both the House and Senate voted to override the veto, so the law took effect.

The bill re-established basic-tier rate regulation where cable systems face no effective competition, prohibited charging subscribers for channels they never ordered, and required carriage of local broadcast and public TV signals.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Cable subscribers came out ahead: rate regulation and billing protections took effect over the industry's objection. Cable operators lost pricing power, while local broadcasters gained guaranteed cable carriage and, through retransmission consent, new bargaining leverage over cable systems.

for.name: Rep. Edward Markey
for.role: House sponsor, member of the Energy and Commerce Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to rein in cable rates after the 1984 deregulation and steer it through the House.

for.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
for.what_they_did: Held markup in June 1992, ordered the bill reported amended, and reported it with H. Rept. 102-628.

for.name: Local broadcast and public television stations
for.what_they_did: Pushed for the must-carry requirement guaranteeing cable carriage of local commercial and educational stations.

against.name: President George H.W. Bush
against.what_they_did: Vetoed the cable bill in October 1992; Congress overrode the veto in both chambers.

against.name: Cable operators and the cable industry
against.what_they_did: Opposed re-regulation of rates and the must-carry mandate and lobbied against the bill.

sides.party_line_note: Passage was bipartisan: 241 of 265 voting House Democrats and 98 of 166 voting Republicans voted yes; the later veto fight split more by party, with congressional Democrats and some Republicans overriding the president.

Retransmission consent, however, lets stations demand payment from cable operators instead, a cost that has largely been passed to subscribers.

industries.industry: Satellite and competing multichannel video distributors
industries.note: Anti-discrimination and refusal-to-deal rules give satellite providers access to programming controlled by cable-affiliated vendors, including a ban on exclusive contracts that deny programming to rural areas without cable, expanding choice and competition.
Compatibility rules require cable signals and converter boxes to work with cable-ready TVs, VCRs, and commercially available remote controls, and bar operators from disabling those functions.
